nameStory: This lichen doesn't have a widely-used common name, so scientists simply call it by its scientific name, Nesolechia oxyspora. The name comes from Greek roots meaning 'island dwelling' (neso-lechia) and 'sharp spore' (oxyspora), referring to its habit of living on other lichens like tiny islands and its distinctive spindle-shaped spores.
description: Nesolechia oxyspora isn't your typical lichen - it's actually a parasitic fungus that lives on other lichens! Instead of making its own food like most lichens do, this sneaky species sets up shop inside leafy and branching lichens, stealing nutrients from its host. You'll spot it as tiny, dark bumps or dots that push through the surface of otherwise healthy-looking lichens, almost like little black pimples on the host's body.

idTips.label: Growth Form
idTips.description: Appears as small, dark, bump-like structures emerging from the surface of host lichens, rather than forming its own independent lichen body

idTips.label: Color
idTips.description: Dark brown to black fruiting bodies that contrast sharply with the usually lighter-colored host lichen

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always found growing on other lichens - never on bare rock, bark, or soil - particularly on leafy and shrubby lichen species

idTips.label: Size
idTips.description: Fruiting bodies are quite small, usually less than 1mm across, looking like tiny dark specks scattered across the host

idTips.label: Surface Texture
idTips.description: Smooth, rounded bumps that feel slightly raised when you run your finger gently over the infected lichen

habitat: Since this species parasitizes other lichens, you'll find it wherever its host lichens grow - on tree bark, rocks, and occasionally soil in forests, parks, and even urban areas throughout New England. Look for it on common foliose lichens growing on oak, maple, and pine trees, as well as on rock-dwelling species in both shaded and partially sunny locations.

seasonality.spring: Dark fruiting bodies become more noticeable as host lichens green up with spring moisture. This is an excellent time to spot the contrast between the parasite and its freshly hydrated host.
seasonality.summer: Fruiting bodies may appear less prominent during dry periods when host lichens are dormant and grayish, but they're still present and identifiable.
seasonality.fall: Another good season for spotting this species as autumn rains reactivate host lichens and create strong color contrasts with the dark parasitic structures.
seasonality.winter: Visible year-round on evergreen substrates, though may be harder to spot when host lichens are dry and less colorful during winter months.

funFact: This tiny parasite is like the ultimate lichen con artist - it can successfully trick and live off at least 63 different lichen species across 19 different groups, making it one of the most adaptable lichen parasites in the world!
confusionNotes: The dark spots could be mistaken for the natural fruiting bodies (apothecia) of the host lichen, but parasite spots are usually smaller, darker, and more irregularly distributed than the host's own reproductive structures. Remember: if the dark spots look out of place or different from the lichen's normal pattern, it's likely this parasite.
contextualKnowledge: This species represents a fascinating example of how the lichen world isn't always cooperative - while most lichens are partnerships between fungi and algae, some fungi have evolved to be freeloaders, exploiting the hard work of established lichen partnerships.
compareHints: Since Nesolechia oxyspora is the only species in its genus found in New England, compare it with other dark, parasitic structures on lichens. Unlike bacterial or other fungal infections that might cause irregular discoloration, this species produces distinctly rounded, bump-like fruiting bodies. It's much smaller and more organized-looking than the irregular black patches caused by other lichen diseases.
